newsitem.title: FRANCE: French franc seen facing pressure after election.
newsitem.headline: French franc seen facing pressure after election.

text.p: The French franc was expected to come under pressure on Monday following Sunday's election in which voters elected a Socialist-led government forced to rely on Communist support for a majority.
But despite what economists called a "worst case result", they said fears of Bank of France intervention would keep the franc from coming under any serious attack.
Expectations of a left win in the parliamentary election had been largely priced into the market and the franc was unlikely to sink below 3.40 per mark in the near term, economists said.
Worries the Bank of France, backed by Germany's powerful Bundesbank, would intervene would keep traders wary of launching any assault on the currency.

"I can see it (the franc) moving toward 3.40 per mark," said economist Paul Horne at Smith Barney in Paris. "But people know the Bank of France has huge resources to defend the franc and can make it extremely expensive to short the franc."
The franc slipped to a low of 3.3840 per mark compared to 3.3816 late on Friday.
The franc has been edging down against the mark since April 17 from near a four-year high of 3.3621 when talk conservative Jacques Chirac would call the snap vote first surfaced.

Mark Geddes, treasury economist at ABN-Amro in London, said there had been "pretty aggressive Bank of France action over the last few weeks to try to limit the downside (for the franc) and I'll expect that to be intensified this week."
Economists were relatively sanguine about the fact the Socialists would have to depend on support from the the Communists to pass legislation.

Jean-Francois Mercier of Salomon Brothers noted that in previous minority situations when the Socialists were in power, the Communists had abstained if they disagreed with a proposed bill rather than vote against the government.
"This would mean that they (the Socialists) could have an absolute majority thanks to Communist abstention," he said.
Alain Galibert, economist at SG Warburg, said he believed Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, who is expected to be named prime minister on Monday, "will multiply his efforts to reassure the markets."

But the election results were nonetheless a "very nice scenario for the dollar and negative for the core euro markets" as it increased chances that the planned single European currency would be a weak one, he said.
He said the outcome was neutral to slightly bearish for the franc against the mark," adding he did not expect the French currency to lose more than one or two centimes against the mark.

The Socialists had signalled they would "definitely govern with an eye on financial markets. They have have made statements in the past week trying to reassure the markets about theier commitment to fiscal discipline," Mercier said.
Geddes said 3.3850 per mark was a key level for the franc and if that were broken, "we could see a move through 3.39. In percentage terms, these are small moves. I would not expect a break of 3.40."
He said Bank of France would likely "get a a helping hand from the Bundesank" if the franc came under heavy pressure.

Economist Marie Owens-Thomsen of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson said election of the Socialists, who advocate a more flexible position on meeting conditions for European monetary union, could damage prospects for a single currency but added "I feel the biggest risk now is from Germany."

The franc stayed relatively stable throughout the election campaign. It was trading at 3.3762 per mark on April 21, the day Chirac called the vote to give him a free hand in the runup to monetary union.
The lowest it traded at during the campaign was 3.3828 on May 28. That was its weakest level since February 4, when it fell to 3.3839 per mark.
